title: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt
goal: By the end you can read a thread's state, wait for a thread with `join()` instead of `sleep()`, and write a worker that stops cleanly when interrupted without losing the interrupt.

warmup.q: A worker is inside `Thread.sleep(10_000)`. Another thread calls `worker.interrupt()`. The worker catches the `InterruptedException`. Inside the catch block, what does `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()` return?
options: true, because it was just interrupted
false, because the flag was cleared when the exception was thrown
It throws a second InterruptedException
It depends on the JVM
warmup.why: Methods that throw `InterruptedException` clear the interrupt flag first. So inside the catch the flag is already false. If the catch block only logs, the stop request is lost for good. That is why the rule is to restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`, or rethrow.

sections.h: A thread is always in one of six states
sections.body:
Call `t.getState()` and you get one of six values of the `Thread.State` enum. Thread dumps print the same names, so learning them now pays off every time you debug a stuck service.

| State | What the thread is doing |
|---|---|
| `NEW` | Created, but `start()` has not been called. |
| `RUNNABLE` | Running, or ready to run and waiting for a core. |
| `BLOCKED` | Waiting to enter a `synchronized` block that another thread holds. |
| `WAITING` | Waiting with no time limit: `Object.wait()`, `join()`, `LockSupport.park()`. |
| `TIMED_WAITING` | The same with a time limit: `sleep(ms)`, `wait(ms)`, `join(ms)`. |
| `TERMINATED` | `run()` has returned or thrown. |

Three of these surprise people.

`RUNNABLE` does not mean "using a CPU". The Javadoc says the thread is executing in the JVM "but it may be waiting for other resources from the operating system such as processor." A thread waiting its turn for a core is `RUNNABLE`. So is a thread stuck in a socket read from Oracle, because the JVM only sees that it is inside native code. A thread dump full of `RUNNABLE` threads can still be a service that does nothing.

`BLOCKED` is only for `synchronized`. A thread waiting for a `ReentrantLock` (lesson 7 of this track) is parked: the lock's own Java code puts it to sleep with `LockSupport.park()` until another thread wakes it, and the JVM reports that as `WAITING`. If you search a dump for `BLOCKED` to find lock contention, you'll miss every explicit lock.

`TERMINATED` is final. A thread cannot be restarted. If you need the work done again, you create a new thread, or better, hand the task to a pool.

sections.h: Wait with join(), because sleep() only passes time
sections.body:
This code waits for a worker, and it is a race:

```java
worker.start();
Thread.sleep(100);          // "should be enough"
use(worker.result);         // may still be unset
```

```kotlin
worker.start()
Thread.sleep(100)           // "should be enough"
use(worker.result)          // may still be unset
```

`Thread.sleep(ms)` pauses the current thread for at least that long and promises nothing about any other thread. On a quiet laptop the worker finishes in 2 ms and the code works. On a loaded CI agent, or a pod sharing its node with a batch job, it doesn't. And even when the worker has finished, `main` is not promised to see `result`. The language gives `sleep` no synchronization meaning, so the JIT may compile both threads as if the other did not exist: it can keep a value in a register instead of memory, or move a read or a write. The memory model track shows a loop that never ends for exactly this reason.

`join()` fixes both problems. It is how one thread waits for another to finish, and it comes in three forms:

```java
t.join();                                          // wait as long as it takes
t.join(500);                                       // wait up to 500 ms, then return either way
boolean ended = t.join(Duration.ofMillis(500));    // JDK 19+: says whether it ended
```

```kotlin
t.join()                                           // wait as long as it takes
t.join(500)                                        // wait up to 500 ms, then return either way
val ended = t.join(Duration.ofMillis(500))         // JDK 19+: says whether it ended
```

After a timed join, check `t.isAlive()` (or the boolean) to learn whether the thread ended or you simply stopped waiting.

`join()` does a second job, and it matters more than the waiting. When `join()` returns, the calling thread is guaranteed to see everything the finished thread wrote. The `java.util.concurrent` docs put it this way: "All actions in a thread happen-before any other thread successfully returns from a join on that thread." Happens-before is the memory model's name for that guarantee. That is why the lab in lesson 1 of this track (Threads from zero) could read the `partial` array after the joins with no locks at all.

Use `sleep` for what it is: a pause. A back-off between retries to the card issuer, or a poll interval. Since JDK 19 you can write `Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(200))` if you like the unit in the type.

sections.h: Daemon threads, and the stop button Java took away
sections.body:
A daemon thread is one the JVM will not wait for. When the last non-daemon thread ends, the JVM exits and any daemon threads stop wherever they are. Their `finally` blocks do not run.

```java
Thread flusher = new Thread(this::flushMetrics, "metrics-flusher");
flusher.setDaemon(true);   // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException
flusher.start();
```

```kotlin
val flusher = Thread(this::flushMetrics, "metrics-flusher")
flusher.isDaemon = true    // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException
flusher.start()            // or in one go: thread(name = "metrics-flusher", isDaemon = true) { flushMetrics() }
```

A new thread copies the daemon setting of the thread that created it, so threads started from `main` are non-daemon. The JVM's own helpers, like `Finalizer` and `Signal Dispatcher` from lesson 1 of this track, are daemons. Daemon threads suit background work you can afford to lose halfway: a cache refresher, a metrics flusher. They are the wrong choice for anything that writes to the ledger or commits a Kafka offset, because the JVM can cut them off between the write and the commit.

So how do you stop a thread that would not finish on its own? You interrupt it, and it stops itself. Java once had a real stop button. `Thread.stop()` threw an error inside the target thread wherever it happened to be, which released its locks and left half-updated objects for other threads to find. It was deprecated in Java 1.2, made to always throw `UnsupportedOperationException` in JDK 20, and removed in JDK 26. `suspend()` and `resume()` were removed in JDK 23. Old code that still calls `stop()` fails with `NoSuchMethodError` on JDK 26 and later.

That leaves cooperative cancellation as the only kind there is: interrupt asks, the thread checks, cleans up and returns. Every executor, framework and pool you use is built on that contract. A task that swallows an interrupt doesn't just ignore one request. It breaks shutdown for every layer above it.

steps: Run `DaemonDemo`. Count the flushes and look for the `finally` line.
Change `setDaemon(true)` to `setDaemon(false)` (in Kotlin, `isDaemon = true` to `false`) and run it again. Stop it with Ctrl+C when you have seen enough.
Keep it non-daemon, and add `metrics.interrupt(); metrics.join();` just before main's last `println`. Run it once more.

code.title: DaemonDemo.java

alt.title: DaemonDemo.kt

try.expect: As a daemon: four flushes, `main: done, returning`, and no `finally block ran`. The JVM exited under it. As a non-daemon it flushes forever, because nothing asks it to stop. With the interrupt and join, it stops at once and prints `finally block ran` before main finishes. That is a clean shutdown.

analogy: Interrupting a thread is like putting a sticky note on a colleague's monitor that says "please wrap up". If they are asleep at their desk (in `sleep` or `wait`), the note wakes them. If they are busy typing, they see it only when they look up, so a good colleague looks up between tasks. The trap is that waking up removes the note: if they read it, shrug and go back to sleep, nobody knows the request was ever made. Restoring the flag means sticking the note back on the monitor for whoever comes next. The analogy breaks because a colleague can ask what you wanted. A thread that clears the flag has no way to recover the request.
in_your_world: Every shutdown in your stack is an interrupt in the end. When Quarkus stops, or Kubernetes sends SIGTERM during a rollout, executors call `shutdownNow()`, which interrupts their worker threads. A Kafka consumer loop that catches `InterruptedException` around a `sleep` back-off and carries on will keep the pod alive until the grace period runs out and the kubelet kills it, possibly halfway through a batch of offset commits. A Temporal activity that retries a card-issuer call with `Thread.sleep` between attempts has the same problem. Search your code for `catch (InterruptedException` and check each one either rethrows or calls `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`.
mistake: The most common real mistake is the empty or log-only catch: `catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted", e); }` inside a loop. People write it because Java forces them to catch the checked exception and the quickest way to make the compiler happy is to log it. Because the flag is cleared when the exception is thrown, the stop request vanishes and the loop runs on. The fix is one line, `Thread.currentThread().interrupt();`, followed by leaving the loop, or declaring `throws InterruptedException` and letting it propagate.

compare.title: An interruptible polling loop in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: KotlinRelay.kt

compare.note: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so `Thread.sleep(50)` compiles without any try/catch. That changes the failure mode. In Java the usual bug is an empty catch that swallows the interrupt. In Kotlin the usual bug is no catch at all: the `InterruptedException` escapes the lambda, the thread dies with a stack trace on standard error, and any cleanup after the loop never runs. Neither is a clean stop. The protocol is the same in both languages: catch it where you can do something sensible, restore the flag, and leave. `isInterrupted` reads as a property in Kotlin, and the static `Thread.interrupted()` still clears the flag.

worked.title: Make a retrying card-issuer call cancellable

steps.say: This retry loop calls the card issuer and backs off on timeouts. Read it and find where a shutdown request disappears.

The inner catch logs and loops. `sleep` cleared the flag before throwing, so nothing remembers the request, and the loop has no limit. If the issuer is down during a rollout, this thread retries until the pod is killed. Before reading on, decide what the method should do when it is interrupted.
Restore the flag first, then stop retrying and tell the caller why. Wrapping the cause in your own exception is fine, as long as the flag is set before you throw. Add a retry limit while you're here.

Now the caller, say an executor shutting down, sees the interrupt flag still set on its worker thread, and the payment is reported as cancelled instead of being retried forever. If `authorize` could simply declare `throws InterruptedException`, that would be even simpler: then there is nothing to restore.

steps: Run the tests. All five fail, and the run is slow, because each test waits 5 seconds for a relay that never stops.

Change the loop condition so it checks `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()` once per batch. Finish the batch in hand before checking.

The "finishes the batch" test counts messages: the total must be a multiple of the batch size. Don't check the flag inside the `for` loop over the batch.

drill.title: Write an interruptible poller from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a `Runnable` that polls a `Supplier<List<String>>` and prints each item. When the list is empty it sleeps 100 ms. It must stop when interrupted, while sleeping or while busy, and leave the flag set when it returns. Then compare.

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: A thread is NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING or TERMINATED. RUNNABLE includes waiting for a core and sitting in native I/O.
BLOCKED means waiting for a `synchronized` monitor. Threads parked on explicit locks show WAITING.
`join()` waits for a thread to end and makes everything it wrote visible to you. `sleep()` does neither.
`interrupt()` only sets a flag. Blocking calls like `sleep`, `wait`, `join` and `take` throw `InterruptedException` and clear the flag first.
When you catch `InterruptedException`, rethrow it or call `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`. Never just log it.
Daemon threads don't keep the JVM alive and can die mid-work. `Thread.stop()` is gone (removed in JDK 26), so cancellation is always cooperative.

quiz.q: A thread is stuck inside `ReentrantLock.lock()`, waiting for another thread to release it. What does `getState()` return?
options: BLOCKED
WAITING
RUNNABLE
TIMED_WAITING
quiz.why: `ReentrantLock` makes waiting threads park with `LockSupport.park()`, and a parked thread is WAITING. BLOCKED is reserved for threads trying to enter a `synchronized` block or method. That difference matters when you scan a thread dump for contention.

options: true
Nothing: the thread sleeps for 5 s and ends
false
It depends on whether interrupt() runs before sleep() starts
quiz.why: If the interrupt arrives during the sleep, `sleep` throws and clears the flag. If it arrives before the sleep starts, `sleep` sees the flag, clears it and throws at once. Either way the catch block sees `false`. Timing changes when the exception comes, not what the flag says.

quiz.q: A Kafka consumer loop wraps its back-off in `try { Thread.sleep(500); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted"); }` and keeps looping. What goes wrong at shutdown?
options: Nothing, because the exception was logged
The consumer stops, but its last batch is processed twice
The JVM throws IllegalMonitorStateException
`shutdownNow()` interrupts it, the catch clears the request, and the loop keeps running until the process is killed
quiz.why: `shutdownNow()` stops tasks by interrupting them. The `InterruptedException` cleared the flag, and the catch block didn't restore it, so the loop never learns it should stop. Logging doesn't count as handling. Restore the flag and leave the loop.

quiz.q: A daemon thread writes audit lines to a file and closes the file in a `finally` block. The last non-daemon thread ends. What happens to the daemon thread?
options: The JVM waits for it to finish the current line
The JVM exits, the daemon stops where it is, and its finally block does not run
The JVM interrupts it and waits for the finally block
It becomes a non-daemon thread and keeps the JVM alive
quiz.why: The JVM does not wait for daemon threads and does not unwind their stacks when it exits, so `finally` blocks don't run. Audit output can be lost or truncated. Work that must complete belongs on a non-daemon thread that you stop with an interrupt and join.

quiz.q: From Threads from zero: a loop starts each thread and joins it in the same iteration, `t.start(); t.join();`, for four threads. While the loop runs, how many of those four threads are alive at the same time?
options: At most one
All four
Two: the current one and the next
None, because join() stops them
quiz.why: Each `join()` blocks the loop until that thread is TERMINATED, and only then does the next iteration start a new thread. So at most one of the four is ever alive. The fix is to start all four first and join them in a second loop.

flashcards.front: A thread waits to enter a `synchronized` block another thread holds. What state is it in?
A thread waits in `ReentrantLock.lock()`. What state is it in?
flashcards.back: WAITING (or TIMED_WAITING for a timed tryLock). Explicit locks park the thread; BLOCKED is only for monitors.
Everything `t` wrote before it ended is visible to the thread whose `join()` returned. `sleep()` gives no such guarantee.

flashcards.front: What happens to the interrupt flag when `sleep()` throws `InterruptedException`?
flashcards.back: It is cleared before the exception is thrown. Inside the catch block, `isInterrupted()` returns false.

flashcards.front: What are the two correct ways to handle a caught `InterruptedException`?
flashcards.back: Rethrow it (declare `throws InterruptedException`), or restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` and stop what you're doing.
`isInterrupted()` only reads the flag. The static `Thread.interrupted()` reads it and clears it.

flashcards.front: What is the status of `Thread.stop()` on JDK 26?
flashcards.back: Removed. It always threw `UnsupportedOperationException` from JDK 20, and old binaries that call it get `NoSuchMethodError` on 26+.

terms.plain: What a thread is doing right now, one of the six values of `Thread.State`.
Wait for a thread to end. Afterwards you see everything it wrote.
A per-thread boolean that `interrupt()` sets to ask the thread to stop.
Thrown by blocking calls when the thread is interrupted. The flag is cleared when it is thrown.
A thread the JVM does not wait for at exit. It can stop mid-work.
Stopping a thread by asking it, and letting it check and clean up itself.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks: "Why can't I just catch InterruptedException and log it? The thread keeps working, so what's the harm?" Answer them in your own words.
explain_back.answer: Interrupt is how the rest of the system asks your thread to stop: executors, shutdown hooks and frameworks all use it. When `sleep` or `wait` throws `InterruptedException`, it clears the interrupt flag first. If you only log, the request is gone and nobody above you can tell it was ever made, so the loop keeps running and shutdown hangs until the process is killed. Either let the exception propagate, or call `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` to put the flag back and then stop what you're doing.

deeper.body:
Not every blocking call listens to interrupts.

`sleep`, `wait`, `join`, `BlockingQueue.take` and `Lock.lockInterruptibly` throw `InterruptedException`. A thread blocked on an NIO `InterruptibleChannel` is different: the Javadoc says the channel is closed, the flag is set and the thread gets a `ClosedByInterruptException`. So interrupting a thread that is writing to a `FileChannel` closes the file for everyone who shares that channel.

Plain `synchronized` does not respond at all. A thread that is BLOCKED waiting for a monitor stays blocked when you interrupt it; only the flag changes. A platform thread reading a classic `java.net.Socket` stream may also sit there until data arrives. For those, set a timeout (a socket read timeout, `tryLock` with a timeout) so the thread wakes up regularly and can check its flag.

Two smaller facts. Interrupts are part of the memory model too: if T1 interrupts T2, everything T1 did before the interrupt is visible to T2 once T2 sees the interrupt (by catching the exception or reading the flag). And JDK 27's Javadoc for `interrupt()` notes that interrupting a thread that is not alive still records the request in the reference implementation, so do not count on an interrupt before `start()` being dropped.
